papers.title: Inferior mesenteric artery morphology and its branching variations: a meta-analysis of 9358 patients with implications for colorectal surgery
papers.authors: Koszewski J, Wilk J, Drozd M, Gliwa J, Plutecki D, Walocha J
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The inferior mesenteric artery (IMA) is a crucial artery that supplies the colon and rectum. As colorectal cancer is most commonly localized in the descending and sigmoid colon, as well as in the rectum, detailed knowledge of the anatomy of the IMA is of utmost importance for oncological surgeons performing hemicolectomies.
METHODS: An extensive search of major databases was performed up to April 2026 for studies detailing the morphometry, anatomy, and variations of the IMA. The study strictly adhered to the PRISMA guidelines. Out of 143,884 initial records, 66 original studies met the inclusion criteria. A random effects model was applied in the statistical analyses, and heterogeneity was evaluated using Chi-squared and I-squared statistics.
RESULTS: The IMA most often originated at the L3 vertebral level (60.35%). The number of sigmoid arteries varied across the study groups, with 2 sigmoid arteries variant being the most common variant at 38.42%, followed by 3 sigmoid arteries variant at 31.30%. Across IMA branching pattern classification systems, the most prevalent anatomical variations were Type 1 in the modified Yada scale (47.39%), Type 1 in Latarjet scale (47.39%), Type 1B in McSweeney scale (45.51%), and Type B in modified Zebrowski scale (20.35%).
CONCLUSIONS: To standardize complex branching patterns, we propose supplementing the modified Yada scale with the exact number of sigmoid arteries for clinical practice, while recommending the McSweeney scale for prospective research. Surgeons must account for significant anatomical variability, as IMA originates at the L3 level in only 60.42% of cases, and the number of sigmoid arteries varies widely, most commonly presenting as two or three. Ultimately, accurate preoperative visualization and standardized IMA categorization are crucial for optimal surgical outcomes.

papers.title: Shared decision making and patient satisfaction in colorectal cancer screening: a multicentric cross-sectional study
papers.authors: Selva A, Torà N, Hortala Bas C, López López P, Machlab S, Burón A
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Colorectal cancer (CRC) screening programs reduce incidence and mortality, but their success depends not only on clinical effectiveness but also on participants' experience and satisfaction. Understanding these dimensions is crucial, as poor satisfaction or limited involvement in shared decision-making (SDM) can undermine uptake and adherence. This study evaluated SDM and satisfaction among participants with a positive fecal immunochemical test (FIT) in an organized CRC screening program in Catalonia.
METHODS: A multicenter cross-sectional study was conducted from November 2020 to December 2021 across three hospitals. Participants aged 50-69 with a positive FIT result were surveyed after colonoscopy and diagnosis. SDM was measured using CollaboRATE and SDM-Q-9; satisfaction was assessed using Hatoum's and Colonoscopy Safety and Satisfaction Questionnaire questionnaires and custom tools. Multivariate analyses identified factors associated with SDM and satisfaction.
RESULTS: Of 846 invited, 824 were included and 694 completed questionnaires (84.2% response rate). Overall, 39.8% achieved the CollaboRATE top score. Higher SDM was linked to shorter wait times, use of Moviprep®,a bowel preparation solution, and absence of complications. Among CRC-diagnosed patients, women and those with a personal cancer history reported higher SDM. Overall satisfaction was high (mean 9.4/10), though bowel preparation scored lowest. Satisfaction varied by hospital, preparation type, and patient characteristics, but not by final diagnosis.
CONCLUSIONS: Participants reported high satisfaction but moderate SDM, revealing room for improvement. Factors such as preparation type, waiting time, and communication quality shaped patient experience. Differences across centers suggest organizational factors matter. Strengthening communication, reducing delays, and addressing patient diversity are essential to enhance satisfaction and engagement, key drivers of CRC screening program effectiveness.

papers.title: Pre-treatment T2WI-based automated artificial intelligence system for predicting neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy response and prognosis in locally advanced rectal cancer: a multicenter study
papers.authors: Sun K, Lu S, Li X, Wang Y, Jiang Z, Wang X
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: In clinical practice, approximately 15-25% of patients with locally advanced rectal cancer (LARC) achieve a pathological complete response (pCR), defined as tumor regression grade 0 according to the AJCC 8th edition, which is closely associated with favorable prognosis. However, noninvasive and accurate preoperative assessment methods remain a major clinical challenge. We aimed to develop an automated artificial intelligence (AI) system for predicting the response to neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy and prognosis in LARC using pre-treatment T2WI.
METHODS: This multicenter retrospective study included 227 LARC patients from Center 1 as the development cohort and 72 and 55 patients from two separate centers as external validation cohorts 1 and 2, respectively. 3D Swin-UNETR was constructed to automatically identify LARC tumors. Based on the segmented tumor volumes, three analytical approaches were implemented to support downstream tasks. Specifically, 1,132 radiomic features (Rf) were extracted using PyRadiomics, while 2,048 deep learning features (Dlf) were derived by 3D ResNet-152 architecture. Following a series of feature selection steps, predictive response scores were generated, including RF scores (Rfs) and Dlf scores (Dlfs). Additionally, an end-to-end analysis was performed to automatically generate Dl scores (Dls). A multi-perspective feature engineering model was then developed by integrating Rfs, Dlfs, and Dls. The predictive performance was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curves (AUROCs). Prognostic indices, including disease-free survival (DFS) and overall survival (OS), were assessed using Kaplan-Meier (KM) analysis, with the Log-Rank test used to compare KM curves.
RESULTS: The fusion model achieved moderate AUROCs of 0.756 and 0.751 in external validation cohorts 1 and 2, respectively. It effectively stratified OS risk, with p-values < 0.05 across all cohorts. For DFS, statistical significance was inconsistent across cohorts, being achieved in the development cohort (p = 0.0084) and external cohort 2 (p = 0.044), but not in external cohort 1 (p = 0.068). These findings are exploratory and require prospective confirmation.
CONCLUSIONS: The proposed AI system demonstrates moderate, externally validated performance for assessing treatment response and OS risk stratification in LARC and may serve as a decision-support tool to assist clinical judgment.

papers.title: Serum vitamins and inflammatory bowel disease in children: a case-control study
papers.authors: Li X, Li T, Wang Y, Li Y, Zhang S, Yan W
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Micronutrient deficiencies are common in pediatric inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), yet data on multiple vitamin profiles remain limited. This study aimed to comprehensively evaluate serum vitamin levels in children with IBD and explore their associations with immune cell profiles.
METHODS: A retrospective observational study was conducted at the Children's Hospital Affiliated to Zhengzhou University. A total of 46 children diagnosed with IBD who had vitamin profiling were enrolled between March 2022 and March 2026. A control group of 46 healthy children, who underwent health check-ups and vitamin assessments during the same period, were also included, matched 1:1 for age and sex. Clinical and laboratory data were retrieved from the hospital's electronic medical record system. Serum levels of vitamins A, D, E, K, B1, B2, B3, B5, 5-methyltetrahydrofolate, and C were measured using ultra-high performance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry.
RESULTS: Compared with controls, IBD patients had significantly lower vitamin A (VA) and vitamin C (VC) levels, while vitamin E (VE) levels were higher (all P < 0.05). Deficiency rates of VA (76.1% vs. 28.3%), VC (50.0% vs. 26.1%), and vitamin D (41.3% vs. 21.7%) were significantly increased in the IBD group (all P < 0.05). Within the IBD cohort, VA, VD, and VC levels correlated significantly with neutrophil and lymphocyte percentages. Multivariate logistic regression identified lower VA level (OR = 0.159, 95% CI: 0.032-0.792, P = 0.025) and VA deficiency (OR = 7.800, 95% CI: 1.735-35.055, P = 0.007) as factors independently associated with IBD.
CONCLUSIONS: Pediatric IBD patients exhibit significant deficiencies in VA, VC, and VD, and within the IBD cohort, these vitamins (VA, VD, and VC) correlate significantly with neutrophil and lymphocyte percentages. Multivariate regression suggests a potential independent association between VA status and pediatric IBD, though these are preliminary observational findings. This study provides preliminary multi-vitamin profiling data for pediatric IBD, highlighting the need for attention to VA and VC deficiencies alongside routine VD monitoring. Further validation in larger multicenter cohorts is required.

papers.title: S100A11 sustains STRAP stability to drive PI3K/AKT/NF-κB feedforward signalling circuit activation in colorectal cancer progression
papers.authors: Li J, Yang H, Xu Z, Dong H, Kou Z, Lu L
papers.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) remains one of the most prevalent malignancies worldwide, with persistently low rates of early-stage diagnosis, poor overall prognosis, and a propensity for therapeutic resistance-challenges that underscore the urgent need for deeper mechanistic insight. By integrating single-cell transcriptomic data (GSE161277) with multi-omics datasets from TCGA and GEO repositories, alongside an independent clinical cohort, we identified S100A11 as a consistently overexpressed gene in CRC that correlates significantly with adverse patient outcomes. Functional studies established that S100A11 drives tumour progression by promoting cell proliferation, suppressing apoptosis, and inducing epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT). Mechanistically, S100A11 engages the WD6-7 domain (residues 221-302) of STRAP through direct physical interaction, thereby recruiting the deubiquitylase OTUB1 to shield lysine K246 of STRAP from K63-linked polyubiquitination. This protection stabilises STRAP and facilitates its association with PI3K, culminating in activation of the PI3K/AKT/NF-κB cascade and nuclear translocation of p65. We further demonstrate that p65 binds directly to the promoter regions of both S100A11 and STRAP, transcriptionally upregulating their expression and establishing a self-reinforcing feedforward loop that sustains pathway activation. Collectively, these findings delineate a hierarchical regulatory network centred on the S100A11/STRAP/NF-κB axis and offer a mechanistic framework with potential implications for CRC diagnosis and targeted intervention.

papers.title: IKK16 and SGI1027 induce cytoplasmic vacuolization, and their combination with chemotherapy drugs can enhance the efficacy of cancer therapeutics
papers.authors: Alsubait A, Alghanem B, Ghadbane H, Huwaizi S, Almuhalhil K, Almourfi F
papers.abstract: Cell death represents a critical process in the maintenance of cellular homeostasis. Paraptosis, a mechanism of programmed cell death, is distinguished by extensive cytoplasmic vacuolization. We have identified two commercially available compounds, IKK16 and SGI1027, which can induce cytoplasmic vacuolization leading to paraptosis in cancer cells. We have characterized and studied various cancer cell lines by applying molecular biology, proteomics, gene expression analyses, and microscopy-based techniques. Additionally, our gene expression analyses indicate that GADD45A, and NPC2 genes may serve as potential markers for identifying paraptosis, and validated their involvement in IKK16/SGI1027-mediated paraptosis with a cellular functional assay. Furthermore, the proteomics data revealed a novel set of proteins previously unassociated with paraptosis. We have substantiated our proteomics findings through western blotting and immunocytochemistry in breast and colorectal cancer cell lines, demonstrating similar effects. Moreover, we have shown that combining paraptosis-inducing compounds with anti-cancer drugs can reduce the required overall dosage concentration while preserving therapeutic efficacy, potentially revolutionizing cancer treatment.

papers.title: Spatial immune architecture and immunotherapy resistance in microsatellite-stable colorectal cancer
papers.authors: Liu X, Liao Q, Cheng Y, Zhou H, Wang R
papers.abstract: Microsatellite-stable (MSS) colorectal cancer (CRC), which accounts for most metastatic CRC, remains largely resistant to immune checkpoint inhibitors. Although low tumor mutational burden and limited neoantigen generation contribute to this resistance, the spatial organization of the tumor microenvironment may also influence antitumor immunity. This review examines mechanisms that establish immune-resistant architectures in MSS CRC, including insufficient T-cell priming, oncogenic signaling, suppressive myeloid niches, hypoxia, abnormal vasculature, and fibroblast-driven extracellular matrix remodeling. We discuss candidate spatial biomarkers, including compartment-specific T-cell distribution, T-cell-tumor-cell distances, multicellular immune neighborhoods, perivascular niches, and the organization and localization of tertiary lymphoid structures. We also examine how fibroblast heterogeneity, collagen architecture, hyaluronan accumulation, and vascular dysfunction can restrict T-cell access and function. Emerging studies associate selected spatial features with treatment outcomes, but the supporting evidence spans small treatment-specific cohorts, mixed CRC populations, and preclinical or non-CRC models. These findings therefore support spatial profiling as a complement to molecular and clinical biomarkers rather than an independently established basis for treatment selection. Prospective studies in defined treatment settings are needed to clarify the relationship between these spatial features and immunotherapy outcomes and to assess their potential to inform combination strategies in MSS CRC.

papers.title: The gut-eye axis in inflammatory bowel disease: shared immune mechanisms and targeted therapies
papers.abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is recognized not only as a disease confined to the intestinal tract, but also as a systemic immune-mediated disorder. Among its diverse extraintestinal manifestations, ocular complications, which range from self-limiting episcleritis to severe and sight-threatening uveitis and scleritis, represent a critical clinical challenge that profoundly impacts patient quality of life. This review synthesizes the epidemiological landscape and clinical spectrum of ocular manifestations in IBD, framing their pathogenesis through the emerging concept of the gut-eye axis. We critically examine the shared mechanistic pathways driving this bidirectional relationship, including the systemic dissemination of circulating inflammatory cytokines, aberrant lymphocyte homing, cross-reactive autoantibodies, shared genetic susceptibilities, and microbiota dysbiosis, which collectively compromise the blood-ocular barrier. Furthermore, we outline targeted therapeutic strategies, highlighting that while systemic anti-TNF agents remain the cornerstone for severe and refractory ocular inflammation, gut-selective biologics like vedolizumab necessitate careful application due to the risk of extraintestinal exacerbation. Finally, we underscore the indispensable role of multidisciplinary management and highlight future research trajectories.

papers.title: CXCR2 associated neutrophil stromal interactions and immune exclusion in microsatellite stable colorectal cancer
papers.abstract: Most microsatellite-stable or mismatch-repair-proficient colorectal cancers respond poorly to immune checkpoint monotherapy. This Mini Review examines whether C-X-C motif chemokine receptor 2 (CXCR2)-associated neutrophil recruitment and local stromal interactions contribute to immune exclusion: CD8+ T cells accumulate in stroma or at the tumor margin with limited entry into epithelial nests. We propose that, in a subset of excluded lesions, recruited neutrophils acquire local functions that impair T-cell activity or access. Human observations and experimental perturbations support parts of this model; the complete pathway has not been established as a major cause of checkpoint resistance. Recruitment dependence, tissue adaptation, and measured function provide a basis for comparing studies with different neutrophil labels. Lesions selected for mechanistic investigation would need confirmed microsatellite-stable or mismatch-repair-proficient status, spatial exclusion, and a relevant intratumoral CXCR2-associated neutrophil program. Primary tumors and metastatic sites require separate evaluation. The limited activity of navarixin plus pembrolizumab argues against unselected targeting. Combining CXCR2 inhibition, selected stromal or vascular modulation, and checkpoint blockade remains a preclinical hypothesis. Before clinical translation, comparative studies must link intratumoral target engagement to improved CD8+ T-cell access, function, and tumor control. The proposed tissue biomarkers are research tools whose predictive value requires validation.

papers.title: Crosstalk between IL-6/JAK/STAT3 and TNF-α/NF-κB signaling in colitis-associated colorectal cancer: epigenetic reprogramming, evidence boundaries, and opportunities for disease management
papers.authors: Yuan J, Liao J, Li F, Xie D, Zuo Z, Zhang D
papers.abstract: Colitis-associated colorectal cancer (CAC) arises through the interaction of chronic mucosal inflammation, genetic evolution and durable changes in gene regulation. Among the inflammatory networks implicated in experimental and human studies, interleukin-6 (IL-6)/Janus kinase (JAK)/signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3) and tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α)/nuclear factor-kappaB (NF-κB) provide mechanistically informative routes by which cytokine exposure can influence DNA methylation, chromatin regulation and non-coding RNA programs. The best-supported examples include IL-6-associated DNMT1 activity and SOCS3 promoter hypermethylation, NF-κB p65/DNMT3A-associated miR-148a methylation, and STAT3-dependent miR-214 induction. These circuits should be regarded as representative mechanisms supported in specific model systems rather than universal initiating pathways in all human CAC lesions. Recent work further demonstrates that colonic stem cells can retain chromatin accessibility changes after experimental colitis resolves, providing direct evidence for durable inflammatory epigenetic memory. This review therefore separates evidence from human CAC or dysplasia, non-neoplastic inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) mucosa, inflammation-driven animal models, sporadic colorectal cancer (CRC) and cell-line systems. We integrate cytokine-linked epigenetic mechanisms with genetic and clonal evolution, define field cancerization operationally, and distinguish persistent epigenetic memory from transient inflammatory transcription. The translational sections are framed as an outlook: no epigenetic biomarker or epigenetic drug is currently established for CAC surveillance or prevention. We summarize the validation requirements for tissue, blood and stool biomarkers; classify therapeutic concepts by evidence level; and propose a patient-level roadmap for single-cell and spatial studies. The resulting framework emphasizes evidence-graded mechanisms and prospective validation rather than assuming that biologically plausible signals are clinically actionable.

papers.title: Overcoming oxaliplatin resistance and toxicity in colorectal cancer: the emerging role of lipid-based nanocarriers
papers.journal_full: The Journal of pharmacy and pharmacology
papers.authors: Chauhan A, Kumar M, Awasthi A
papers.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To provide a comprehensive overview of lipid-based nanocarriers for oxaliplatin (OXA) delivery in colorectal cancer (CRC), with emphasis on their potential to improve pharmacokinetics, enhance tumour accumulation, enable controlled drug release, and overcome OXA resistance.
METHODS: Relevant literature on OXA, CRC, lipid-based nanocarriers, drug resistance, tumor targeting, co-delivery, and stimuli-responsive delivery systems was reviewed. The review focused on liposomes, solid lipid nanoparticles (SLNs), nanostructured lipid carriers (NLCs), lipid micelles, and advanced lipid-based systems, including passive and active targeting strategies and approaches for overcoming therapeutic resistance.
KEY FINDINGS: Lipid-based nanocarriers demonstrated potential to improve OXA delivery through enhanced tumour accumulation, controlled release, prolonged drug exposure, and improved intracellular uptake. Active targeting using folate, CD44, peptides, or antibodies, along with co-delivery, tumor microenvironment modulation, and externally triggered release, may further enhance therapeutic efficacy and help overcome multidrug resistance. However, most evidence remains preclinical, and challenges including formulation stability, tumor heterogeneity, large-scale manufacturing, and regulatory requirements limit clinical translation.
CONCLUSIONS: Lipid-based nanocarriers represent a promising strategy for improving OXA therapy in CRC, particularly for addressing toxicity, drug resistance, and inefficient tumor delivery. Nevertheless, the limited clinical evidence for OXA-loaded lipid nanocarriers necessitates further pharmacokinetic, toxicological, manufacturing, and well-designed clinical studies before their clinical effectiveness can be established.

papers.title: From Mechanism to Management: The Link Between Inflammatory Bowel Disease and Cardiovascular Disease
papers.authors: Yasmin F, Ahmed M, Bin Iftikhar T, Rab A, Qazi M, Asghar M
papers.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Inflammatory bowel diseases (IBDs) constituting the ulcerative colitis (UC) and Crohn's disease (CD) primarily affect the gastrointestinal tract and have been associated with the development of cardiovascular disease (CVDs). To strengthen this further, the focus of our narrative review is to highlight the clinical significance of understanding this association.
METHODS: We conducted a narrative review to discuss the mechanisms of pathogenesis underlying the link between the management of inflammatory bowel disease and cardiovascular disease.
DISCUSSION: The pathogenesis of the link likely involves dysregulated immune responses leading to overactivation of pro-inflammatory cytokines, suggesting a shared inflammatory pathway. Both diseases share common risk factors such as obesity, diabetes, and gender. Genetic factors, including mutations in NOD2 and CDKN2A, also play a role in the overlap between IBDs and CVDs. Despite the recent developments, conventional cardiovascular risk assessment tools may not fully capture the potential elevated cardiovascular threat in IBD patients.
CONCLUSION: Thus, proactive investigation with advanced diagnostic tools such as coronary artery calcium (CAC) scoring is crucial in reducing cardiovascular morbidity and mortality in these patients. Nevertheless, future research is needed to further clarify disease activity and its correlations.
CLINICAL TRIALS REGISTRATION: NA.

papers.title: Molecular mechanisms of colorectal cancer: from carcinogenesis and molecular classification to targeted therapy
papers.authors: Aldeyarbi S, Elhanafy E, Saber-Ayad M, Abu Almaaty A, Sagheer A, Hassan M
papers.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is a heterogeneous disease that results from the progressive accumulation and interactions at multiple levels of genetic alterations, which lead to the transformation of normal colonic epithelium into malignant colorectal tumors. Understanding the molecular basis of CRC pathogenesis, together with the interactions between genetic alterations, epigenetic modifications, environmental and lifestyle factors, is essential for improving prevention, diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment strategies. This review aims to provide a critical reference point for understanding the temporal dynamics of colorectal carcinogenesis, the evolution of molecular classification systems, including their computational and machine-learning foundations and emerging image-based prediction approaches, molecular drivers and the tumor microenvironment (TME) of CRC by summarizing the most investigated molecular pathways involved in CRC pathogenesis and their role as biomarkers for early CRC diagnosis based on the three main molecular mechanisms of colorectal carcinogenesis: chromosomal instability (CIN), microsatellite instability (MSI), and CpG island methylator phenotype (CIMP). Importantly, emerging evidence reveals that the TME acts as an important factor in driving CRC progression by regulating the immune system through dynamic cellular and molecular interactions. In particular, tumor metabolic reprogramming and microbiota-driven alterations act as major drivers of therapy resistance and immune escape. Combining these mechanisms will enhance biomarker discovery and aid in developing precision medicine for patients with CRC. This review also highlights the regulatory roles of key signaling pathways, including Wnt/β-catenin, epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), tumor protein p53 (TP53), and transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β) signaling, during CRC initiation and progression, while further addressing current targeted therapies and emerging precision-based and experimental therapeutic strategies.
